questions.prompt: A brochure offers a cottage by the sea "for a fortnight in July". How long is the stay?
questions.explanation: A fortnight is exactly "two weeks", fourteen nights, and it is the word a British brochure uses for the standard summer let. "one week" is half of it, and English calls that simply a week. "five days" is shorter still and matches no fixed word at all. "one month" is more than twice a fortnight; the word for that is a month. The trap is to hear fort- and think of four, which would give four weeks.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The coast path runs ___ the shoreline for two kilometres, and the sea is never out of sight."
questions.explanation: The path follows the line of the coast and keeps the sea beside the walker the whole way, and the preposition that follows the line of something is "along". "across" takes you from one side of a surface to the other, so the path would cross the coast and leave it, which is exactly what the second half of the sentence denies. "through" needs something you go into on one side and come out of on the other, such as a tunnel or a wood, and a shoreline is a line, not a space. "off" says you leave the way you were on, which no path does to itself.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The eastern beach is ___ quieter than the one beside the port."
questions.explanation: quieter is already a comparative, and the words English puts in front of a comparative to strengthen it are much, far, a lot and many more, which gives "far" quieter than the one beside the port. "very" is the one modifier English refuses in front of a comparative, however natural it sounds to a French or an Arabic ear. "more" doubles the comparison, since the -er of quieter already carries the idea that more would add. "most" is the mark of a superlative, and a superlative cannot stand in a sentence that goes on with than.

questions.prompt: Read: "When the family reached the cottage, the storm had already cut the electricity." In which order did the two things happen?

options.text: The electricity went off first, and the family arrived after that.
The family arrived first, and the electricity went off after that.
The family arrived, and the electricity went off the next morning.
The two things happened at exactly the same moment.

questions.explanation: Of the two verbs, reached is a simple past and had cut is a past perfect, and the past perfect always marks the earlier of two past events, whatever order the sentence prints them in: "The electricity went off first, and the family arrived after that." "The family arrived first, and the electricity went off after that." reads the sentence in the order of the words instead of the order of the tenses, which is the whole trap. "The family arrived, and the electricity went off the next morning." pushes the storm to a later day, but already says it was over before they walked in. "The two things happened at exactly the same moment." would need one single tense for both halves.

questions.prompt: In a letter of complaint a traveller has already described two problems. She now brings in the third and last one, and she wants to say that it matters as much as the others. Which phrase opens it?
questions.explanation: "Last but not least," introduces the final item of a list and states in so many words that it is not the least important of them, which is precisely the double job she needs. "At last," expresses relief when something long awaited finally arrives, and nothing here has been waited for. "Eventually," reports how a process ended after a while, so it would announce an outcome rather than a third complaint. "In the first place," opens a list, and her list has been open for two problems already.
